title: HTTP Methods & Status Codes
subtitle: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE — when to use each, and what responses mean
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: HTTP has multiple request methods, but developers often default to GET and POST for everything — creating ambiguity and non-standard APIs.
whyItExists.solution: Each HTTP method has a defined semantic: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes. Using the right method makes APIs self-documenting, enables caching, and allows idempotent operations.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every time you design or call an API endpoint — choose the method that matches the operation's semantic meaning, not just what works.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Some environments (old browsers, certain proxies) only support GET and POST. In those cases, tunnelling via POST with a method override header is common.

explainModes.beginner: HTTP methods describe what you want to do: GET = please give me data. POST = here is new data, save it. PUT = replace this existing record with this. PATCH = update only these specific fields. DELETE = remove this record. Using the right method matters because it tells the server (and caches, and developers) exactly what the request does.
explainModes.simple: GET: safe, cacheable, no body. POST: creates, has a body, not idempotent. PUT: full replace, idempotent (same call twice = same result). PATCH: partial update, body has only changed fields. DELETE: removes resource, idempotent. HEAD: like GET but response has no body — just headers (check if resource exists without downloading it). OPTIONS: asks what methods are allowed (used by CORS preflight). Safe = no side effects. Idempotent = multiple identical requests = same state as one.
explainModes.standard: Idempotency matters: POST is NOT idempotent — submitting a form twice creates two records. PUT IS idempotent — uploading the same file twice leaves you with the same file. PUT vs PATCH: PUT requires sending the complete resource (missing fields get nulled). PATCH sends only changes — more efficient, but servers must handle partial updates carefully. Status code families: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (your fault), 5xx server error (their fault). 429 Too Many Requests: you've hit a rate limit — back off and retry. Retry-After header tells you how long to wait.
explainModes.technical: Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS): MUST not change server state. This is a semantic guarantee — caches and intermediaries rely on it. Idempotent methods (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS): multiple identical requests produce the same server state as a single one. Allows safe retries after network failures. POST is neither safe nor idempotent — retrying POST can create duplicate resources (use idempotency keys: a unique ID in a header like Idempotency-Key: uuid, server stores it and returns the same response if seen again). CONNECT: establishes a tunnel (used for HTTPS through proxies). TRACE: diagnostic — server echoes the request back.
explainModes.deepDive: HTTP method override: some frameworks check for an X-HTTP-Method-Override header on POST requests to simulate PUT/PATCH/DELETE for clients that can't send them. Content-Type negotiation: POST/PUT/PATCH body format is declared by Content-Type header — application/json, multipart/form-data, application/x-www-form-urlencoded are the three common types. Server-Timing header: returned by servers to expose backend timing — useful for performance debugging. Structured field values (RFC 8941): standardized format for complex HTTP header values.

content.text: Use PATCH (not PUT) for most updates — it's more efficient since you only send the fields that changed. PUT is for replacing an entire resource (like uploading a file), where you always have the complete new version.

questions.question: You call DELETE /users/42 twice. What happens on the second call?
options: The user is deleted again — DELETE can be called multiple times
The second call returns 404 Not Found (user no longer exists), but the server state is the same as after the first call — this is what 'idempotent' means
The second call returns 200 OK with the deleted user data
The second call causes a 500 Server Error
questions.explanation: DELETE is idempotent: the server state after the second call (user is gone) is identical to the state after the first call. However, the response code differs — 404 is correct for the second call since the resource no longer exists. Idempotent means the *state* is the same, not necessarily the response code. This is useful for retrying requests after network failures: you know retrying DELETE is safe.

faq.q: When should I use PUT vs PATCH?
faq.a: Use PATCH for most updates — you send only the fields you want to change: `{ "email": "new@example.com" }`. The server merges these into the existing record. Use PUT when replacing a complete resource — you must send all fields, and missing fields get their default/null values. A common example of PUT: uploading a file (you always send the full file). PATCH is better for record updates since you don't need to fetch the full object first.

examples: GitHub: PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo} — update repo description without touching other settings
Stripe: POST /payment_intents — creates a payment (not idempotent, uses Idempotency-Key header for safety)
S3: PUT /bucket/key — uploads a file (full replace, idempotent)
